newsitem.title: FRANCE: France seeks review of EU veal aid after protest.
newsitem.headline: France seeks review of EU veal aid after protest.

text.p: France said on Monday it wanted a review of European Union aid for veal producers hit by the mad cow crisis after French cattle breeders ransacked Dutch trucks and burnt meat cargoes in an anti-EU protest.

Agriculture Minister Philippe Vasseur said he would put the protesters' case to an EU farm ministers' meeting in Brussels on Tuesday. "It's true there is a distortion" of the market under EU subsidies, he told France Info radio.

About 800 French breeders, who say that EU aid favours Dutch and Belgian farmers, seized veal carcasses from four Dutch trucks and incinerated the meat on bonfires at the Rungis wholesale market south of Paris overnight on Monday.

Officials at the market said one Irish truck was also hit. But Gerard Barbin, administrator of the National Bovine Federation (FNB) that organised the protest, said he was unaware of demonstrators targeting Irish cargoes.
Police at the market declined comment.

"There were no arrests and no confrontations with police," said Philippe Stisi, a spokesman for the Rungis market. The breeders, who came in about 20 buses from western and southwestern France, left on Monday.

The FNB also said it aimed to file suit at the European Court over the EU subsidies. "We want to prove that the measure is unjust," Barbin told Reuters. Barbin and other breeders were received by officials at the Agriculture Ministry.
The new subsidies are to encourage the slaughter of calves younger than usual to cut the amount of beef on an EU market depressed by the mad cow crisis that has hit British herds hardest.
The subsidies go to producers who cut 15 percent off the average normal weight of calves at slaughter -- but the average varies from country to country.

Dutch breeders, whose calves usually weigh more than 160 kg (350 lbs), get a subsidy for producing a calf of 138 kg (300 lbs) or less, for instance, while the French producers only qualify with calves weighing 108 kg (240 lbs) or less.
Calves skinny by Dutch standards sell well in France because they are about the size of calves normally marketed in France, Barbin said.

The EU imposed a ban on British beef exports in March after the British government disclosed that the disease, known medically as Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), could spread to people who ate infected beef.
